utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've just been handed the clip of documents. Mr. Agha, the sittings today -- let me deal with this formally at the outset. It may well be that we will have the courtroom this afternoon, which will enable us to sit into the afternoon. I'm going to get a message. Just one moment. We'll confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What we propose is this: That we will sit in the afternoon. We'll sit for the first session for an hour and a half, we will break for half an hour, we will then have another session of an hour and a half, we will break then for the lunch break for one hour and a half, and then we'll sit in the afternoon from 2 to 3.30, and that way we can accommodate the work. Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As I heard it was a proposal, can I just make an observation, because I have to comply with various administrative procedures within the Tribunal, and my attendance here was arranged so that I left Holland this afternoon in the afternoon, leaving this building at 2.15, which helps with the economy of the case. If any legal argument on the intercepts could be heard this morning rather than this afternoon, that would assist everyone greatly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll accommodate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we'll have the legal argument, since you might be involved in it, then in the second session, I should think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Agha.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This witness is a 92 bis witness, so I kindly ask that a pseudonym sheet be placed before him.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Witness, could you please confirm that is your name on that sheet and that you signed and dated it, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Witness, you also gave a statement before the Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Agha, we need, for the record formally, the witness's pseudonym for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Witness is B-1011.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you would go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Witness, you gave a statement before the Tribunal in September of 1998, which was certified by the Registry on 18 November 2001; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Can his bis package be kindly placed before the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Witness, can you please confirm that that is in fact your statement signed by you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And may I kindly ask for that 92 bis package to be exhibited if it's not already been so already.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 614, Your Honour, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And could we also please have an exhibit number for the pseudonym sheet, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It can be included in the package.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As I mentioned earlier, Your Honours, this witness is a 92 bis witness from Brcko municipality, and I shall briefly read out a summary of his evidence. Prior to the war, the witness was neither a member of the SDS or SDA and had no political affiliation. Between the night of the 30th of April and 1st of May, the bridges were blown up in the Brcko area, and the various Serb paramilitary groups started to carry out an offensive on Brcko. The witness took refuge in his sister's cellar, and after Brcko was taken by the Serbian forces, they came round the various houses. The witness was taken out of the cellar with the others he was hiding with and they were separated on the basis of ethnicity. The witness and his group were marched to the SUP building where he came across a JNA captain who ordered them to be taken to the Posavina Hotel. The man who had carried out the separation was known as Dragan, with an English-sounding accent and was in charge of the Serb forces who had taken him out of the house and taken him to the hotel. At the hotel, he saw four dead bodies out of the window, all of which had been piled on top of each other and were wearing civilian clothes. They looked as if they had been recently killed. In the hotel, a local man called Goran Jelisic then entered the room with a lady called Monika. Jelisic then started beating up a man with water bottles. There were about 25 men detained in the room, and they were soon shifted to the hotel terrace. They were made to stand up in two lines and Jelisic began to beat two of the men. An older man was then thrown amongst the group and was also being beaten. When he complained, he was taken out of the group and shot. A Croat amongst the group was released because he was in the same house as the witness, whereupon on the basis of being in the same house the witness and another Muslim was able to secure his release. He was sent to a park. Whilst he was in the park, the witness was about 50 metres away, and he turned instinctively, and he saw Jelisic standing there with a handgun, gunfire burst, and bodies falling. He was then shepherded to the SUP building where he was told not to look at anything, and he heard five or six more shots. After answering a few questions, the witness was released. A few months later, he was arrested and taken to the Batkovic camp. Now, that is the essence of the witness's evidence, and if I may, with the Court's permission, ask the witness a few questions orally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Witness, if you can please answer these questions I ask you. Prior to the attack on Brcko, can you tell the Chamber whether anyone had been arming, any group had been arming the local population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: As far as Serbs are concerned, yes, they were armed. That much I know. As for the rest of the population, individual people procured weapons if they could afford it.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... group or body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: They got weapons directly from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, when the Serb paramilitary forces had taken over Brcko, where did they stay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Paramilitary forces in Brcko that had arrived in mid-April 1992 had their headquarters within the JNA garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, while they were staying there, were there JNA officers or soldiers there or was it empty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: The command staff of the JNA was together with them in the same rooms on the same premises of the garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Were these regular JNA soldiers or reservists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Active-duty commanding officers were in the garrison in Brcko. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And how do you know this, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: I passed by every day. I live in the neighbourhood, and I had occasion to see it with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about a different person, a person you mention as Dragan in your statement. Where did he and his men come from? Were they local?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: No. Captain Dragan, whom I recognised and he himself introduced himself as Captain Dragan, had come from the direction of Bijeljina, accompanied by all those who were with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about your treatment in Batkovic. Were you treated well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Well, it all depended on individual people, on individual prisoners, and on those who were on duty and in charge of taking people out to be beaten. As for me personally, I have permanent scars that are visible, and I can say again that I was lucky, actually, because I was among those who were beaten the least.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... just like to place a picture on your monitor and ask if you can identify the person in the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And for the Chamber, this has been previously tendered as an exhibit, which is 347, tab 7.5.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Do you recognise who that is? Could you tell the Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes. That is Captain Dragan precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And is that the same Dragan you saw in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: That would conclude the evidence in chief, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. 1011, in paragraph 3 of your statement, you state that the conflict in Brcko began in the night of the 30th of April; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: That's when the offensive began to take over the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was happening before that when you say the offensive began on that night to take the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: I want to explain exactly how it began. In the middle of the month of April, a session of the Municipal Assembly of our town was convened, attended also by some foreign delegates. I think they were from Sweden. That session took place in the cultural hall of Brcko. An explicit demand was made then by the Serb side, headed by Dr. Beli, to divide the town. The advice of the foreign observers was to refrain from doing that and to try instead to find some common language. The session was postponed by 20 days. A new session was supposed to take place on the first workday after the May holidays. All schools in town stopped working; children were relieved of school. And in the meantime, I don't know whether it was from Serbia or from Belgrade that some military police came in order to introduce some order into the town, quote unquote, to prevent incidents, and among them was this captain who arrived. And indeed he started immediate action to replace all non-Serbs from their managerial and senior positions. He was accompanied by people and troops with special training and under full military gear, including camouflage uniforms, bulletproof vests. They wore automatic rifles in front, and on their backs they had one to two hand-held rocket launchers, Zoljas. And these men toured the town. That's what I can say about the beginnings. The incidents that had begun to occur in the town after that first session in the middle of April until the time when paramilitary formations entered our town officially on the 4th of May and occupied the town up to the Brka river which borders our town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Witness 1011. Did any incidents happen? Was anybody injured? Until then, was that captain the same Captain Dragan you mentioned or some other captain?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: No. I saw Captain Dragan on the 4th and 5th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this one was another captain?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes. This man wore a regular military uniform, and he even spoke on the local television.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did he say on local television?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: He said that he had been sent to our town to prevent conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he said on local television that the JNA was there to prevent incidents in view of the atmosphere reigning in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes. Due to the atmosphere that began to prevail in town after the Serb side demanded that the town be divided.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So after that session of the Assembly which you say was attended by Swedes as well, what was the situation in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there were no incidents, a session of the Assembly was held sometime in April; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And at that session there happened the first incident with a demand to divide the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes. The Serbs, and I can't mention -- I can't remember the name of the man who made the demand, I think it was Dr. Beli, who was a doctor, made the demand to divide the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was his position in the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: He was the president of the Serb party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who was the president of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Mr. Ramic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who is vice-president and president of the executive council of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I'm not quite sure and I wouldn't like to say anything because I can't say it with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But do you have an explanation as to why this Dr. Beli, who is president of the party, wanted the town divided? What did he give as an explanation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: He didn't say anything. It was simply the position of the Serb side that the town should be divided. I cannot tell you specifically what he wanted to achieve by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us not dwell on it any further then. Since you claim that this Serb offensive ended on the 4th of May --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: No. It officially began on the 4th of May and the town was taken over, occupied, up to the Brka River which divides the left and the right side of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you because I can't really understand from your statements. You say that the war in Brcko began in the night of the 30th of April, and now you say that it began on the 4th of May. You say actually in your statement that it was on the night of the 31st of April. The 31st of April does not exist. I suppose you mean the 30th of April.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: I will explain this as well now. The bridges were blown up during the night. It was just the first sign that the session that was supposed to take place after the May holidays would not take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand this. What did the bridges have to do with the session?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: To me, it was a clear sign that the session had better not take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who blew the bridges up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: It's sad, but I have to say it. It's a man who had come from Serbia some 15 years earlier, got married and lived there, and he is still there today. He's one of the ministers in Municipal Assembly of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you mean that he was a resident of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It doesn't matter where he had come from. You say that he had lived in Brcko for 15 years and he was a resident of that town.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why did he blow up the bridges? Which bridges?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: There are two bridges in Brcko across the Sava River linking Bosnia with Croatia. One is a railroad bridge exclusively, and the other bridge is both a freight and a passenger bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Croatian forces make any incursions over those bridges before that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Not that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any arms deliveries using those bridges from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: I stated and I wrote in my statement that I was not involved with any political party, and I did not interfere with politics in any way, and that includes arms deliveries and such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I believe, Mr. 1011, that you did not interfere with politics. I'm only asking you what you know about this. A politically uninvolved resident of Brcko can know something about it. I'm asking you, what was the reason for blowing up the bridges that connect Bosnia with Croatia? Because you even know who blew them up. You say it was a man who was still -- who is still there occupying an important position.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm saying that it's a sad thing that this man who had done such a thing is still there in Brcko. And as for the bridges, before they were destroyed from the Bosnian side had been made useless from the Croatian side, because they are about 800 metres long.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose it was not this man from Brcko who made them useless. Who did that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: The Croats from that side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So those bridges were actually already destroyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Well, they were made useless in terms of transporting freight or passengers. Instead, some kind of pontoon bridge or maybe hanging bridge was made so that only pedestrians could use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you say that they were already destroyed by the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: They were made useless.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that much. Was anyone injured at the time? Did anything else happen? And third, how do you know that this man you are referring to was the one who destroyed those bridges who had -- which had already been made useless?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: You mean from our side?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. How come that you know the person who allegedly demolished these bridges?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: The person. I found out directly from his colleagues, his partners who helped him carry out this task, this assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you find that out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: A couple of years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you are testifying to something that you learned about several years after the event you are speaking to in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: It's sad that I have to say it, but I'm saying it with deep conviction: I believe the person who recounted it to me told the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I do not doubt your deep conviction, but you found that out from somebody who told you about it several years later.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. 1011. But tell me, since you say the war began in the night of the 31st of April - I suppose it is the 30th of April - and that on the 4th Serb forces occupied a part of Brcko, does it mean that there was some fighting that lasted for four days or is it something that eludes me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Let me be brief and clear. On the 4th of May in the morning, as far as I could notice and to the extent to which I moved about at that time, I managed to count 22 people in uniform or, rather, 22 different types of uniforms; active police, reservists, JNA reservists, all sorts of volunteers, and so on. There was shooting too. But people were shooting only in order to reach the area that they wanted to reach as soon as possible. That means that they came to the Brka river which divides the town into the left-hand side and the right-hand side, they tried to advance further, they were stopped there. Because their general interest was to reach the Belgrade-Banja Luka road. That's the only road that goes through Brcko. They were stopped there by various groups that were engaged on their own. They tried to get their families out and to get them away from the gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. What were these different groups? Were these some kind of Muslim armed forces? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: These were groups consisting of up to five or six people that were organised in that way, and that's how they operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a second, Mr. 1011. A few minutes ago you said that you saw 22 different types of the military. They went to take the other side, and then they were stopped by groups of five or six men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Sir, please do not confuse things. I said it very nicely. Twenty-two different types of the military that came to take the town. That's what I saw. And when they tried to cross the Brka river in order to take the other part of town, they were stopped there by these men who usually had hunting weapons only.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. So you're trying to say that these 22 different types of the military that were trying to cross the river were stopped by a group of five or six men who had hunting weapons; right? Is that what you're saying, Mr. 1011?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Let's make this clear. Not all 22 types of the military were crossing the river in order to take this notorious corridor between Belgrade and Banja Luka. These were individual groups with this well-known person from the area around Bijeljina who had come too. That is Goran Jelisic. He headed all the offensives that were launched across the Brka River.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And they did not succeed because they were stopped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: They did not succeed on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. However, Brcko spreads to the other side of the river too, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And they did not take the area on the other side of the Brka River because they had been stopped.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Not on that day. I'm talking specifically about the 4th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If they were not stopped on that day, when did they manage to take it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: A few days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, a few days later. All right. In paragraph 5, you say that you were arrested in your sister's house together with 30 other persons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: No. No, not 30 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Do you need an explanation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. There's no need for an explanation. You sought shelter there from combat, in the cellar. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of combat was this? Is that the combat involving these people who were on different sides of the Brka River?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: I can explain this to you. These were groups of men who were armed. Specifically in my case, a group came consisting of, say, about 15 to 20 men. They came on a fire truck in the street where I was, and different people came out wearing different kinds of uniforms too. They were led by Captain Dragan personally, and they went from one house to the other, and they threw everyone out. The men were separated, all men. In my case, there were about 30 of us that were taken out of all these houses, and we were taken to the police station, in front of the police station, rather. It's not even 50 metres away from the Hotel Posavina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. 1011, you say that Captain Dragan came to the house.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that he wore different kinds of -- different kinds of clothing, namely civilian trousers, jeans, and a military jacket and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. boots.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were just shown his picture now and you said that's what he looked like, but we see that in the photograph he is wearing a uniform. He's not wearing jeans.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: It's not according to the clothes. I recognised him by his face.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, by his face.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes. I can even describe what he looks like, how he talks, how he walks. I have a lasting memory of what he looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You wrote here -- I mean, I'm trying to save time. You say that he was around 45, that he was thin and tall, that he had short hair, and that he had an English-sounding accent. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he was tall and thin and about 45 years old?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Well, approximately. I mean, I didn't look at his ID, but I think that that was his approximate age at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the photograph he wore a cap. Since you established that he had short hair, he probably did not wear a cap then.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: When he came to see us -- or, rather, when he came to see me, he had that cap that we call a jockey cap. It is sort of like a baseball cap. He also wore dark glasses. When he introduced himself, when he said what his name was, he asked us, "Do I look like an American or a gangster?" All of us who there said yes. And he swore at America and Americans, and he threw off his cap and his glasses, and that's how I could see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was his hair blonde or dark?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Well, brownish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since he testified here, everybody could see first and foremost that he -- his hair is grey. It's not blonde, and it's not dark. Also, he's a short man. He cannot be described as a tall man by any standards, not even medium height.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: You're wrong, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed. Also, you said that he had an English-sounding accent. Do you speak English?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How can you conclude then that he had probably been in Australia? On what basis do you come to that conclusion? In all fairness, people do speak English in Australia, and perhaps somebody who speaks English really well can distinguish between different accents, including an Australian accent. How did you come to the conclusion that he was from Australia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: I did not come to this direct conclusion. I assumed that he could have been a member of a special unit or someone who at that time was involved in all sorts of things, even that he was in the Foreign Legion. That was my assumption. And later on, it proved to be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. 1011. Are you talking about things here that could have been read in the newspapers later about Captain Dragan? He talked about it here. He testified about it here, that he came from Australia, and so on and so forth. Tell me, when you saw him, how could you have concluded that he might have been in the Foreign Legion and that he came from Australia, and most of all that he was tall? That is the last thing that you can claim.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Please. I know that I'm a person of medium height, and he is taller than I am, and that was my yardstick. As far as his accent is concerned and the way he speaks and whether I noticed that he sounded English or not, I think that you can hear that until the present day. His speech is not clear, he is not very fluent. As for whether I knew him personally, I'm not interested in him as a person at all. I felt no need to see him afterwards. I survived what I survived. Now, what he did before and what he did later is something I don't know, but I do know what he did on that day, on the 4th and even on the 5th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right; I didn't ask you about that, what you are claiming that he did. I asked you to tell me on the basis of what you concluded that he was in the Foreign Legion and that he was in Australia -- that he had been in Australia. How could you conclude that when you saw him on the 4th of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: I made a statement pertaining to the 4th of May. My assumption was that he had come from somewhere. He came back. Later on, it so turned out. At that moment I did not know it myself until he introduced himself to us. I didn't know who he was and where he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did he introduce himself to you that way, that he had come from Australia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: He personally said that he came from the area of Bor and Majdanpek. That is what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did he say that he came from Australia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you concluded that he came from Australia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: I think that I was quite clear when I talked about this. After some time, I came to know that he had come from Australia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, you learnt about it subsequently. You could have read about it in the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how much later did you find out about him coming from Australia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: If you want me to be very precise, in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So a year later?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You learned about it from the newspapers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you gave your statement in 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And now, five years later, you claim that this was Captain Dragan, because here you say that this man's name was Dragan, that he came, et cetera, et cetera. You do not say "Captain Dragan" in the statement. Is that right, Mr. 1011, in your statement of 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: I stated what he said to us and what he said by way of an introduction. No, it is possible that there are some mistakes involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So five years after you gave your statement, you managed to state that it was Captain Dragan.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: I'm perfectly sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many times did you see him on television? How many times did you see his picture similar to the one shown to you a moment ago and various other photographs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: I told you already that I'm not interested in him as a person at all. I have absolutely no problem with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. If you have absolutely no problem with him and you are not interested in him, then why in 1998, when you were giving your statement, didn't you mention that it was Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: What do you mean I didn't say so? I said so right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, find that place in your statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Maybe it was an omission made during the typing and printing, but I said word-for-word that Captain Dragan was a person I saw personally with my own eyes on the 4th and the 5th of May. He took me out of my home together with many other people when he was going from house to house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in your statement, you mention only Captain Petrovic, a captain of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes. That's the officer who came.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This officer who said on television that he had come to prevent clashes, conflicts, and disturbances.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes. He made his statement on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's the only captain you mention in your statement of 1998. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: He's an active duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mention also many other names but without mentioning the rank. You mention Dragan only as Dragan, not as a captain.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: That's how he introduced himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you write that in your statement then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: I didn't write my statement. I didn't type it. Maybe the person who typed it omitted the word "Captain."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. 1011. In paragraph 7, you say that in the course of your arrest this man was accompanied by a group of 30 men.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: I'm saying this once again: Not 30. Dragan came with two men and rounded us up. He collected 30 people or so from the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at paragraph 7 of your statement. In the middle of the paragraph there is a sentence that says: "There was a group of 30 or so other soldiers that was in the area also going to the various houses and rounding people up."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "The other soldiers wore different military uniforms and they all had firearms." Tell me if there is some mistake here.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: No, it's perfectly all right. I agree with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the people you were talking about were not uniformly dressed. They had different uniforms.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes. It's exactly how I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Do I need to describe how they were dressed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No thank you. You gave a detailed description already. You said they wore different uniforms. Let us clear one thing up: On the basis of this description that you provided, isn't it crystal clear that those were not members of the JNA? They could have been members of a volunteer unit or some other unit, but people who were not uniformly dressed, who wore all sorts of uniforms, could not have been JNA.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: They were indeed dressed as I described.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But tell me, would you say that the reserve force was not part of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, even the reserve force of the JNA wore JNA uniforms. You must know that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Even reservists didn't wear civilian clothes mixed with military uniform. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: I don't want to argue with you. All those people, 30 of them or so, wore different uniforms. Not more than two wore the same uniform, and some of them wore even reservists uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You just said that no more than two wore the same uniform. Isn't that the best proof that it couldn't have been the JNA if out of 30 only two wore the same uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: That's your conclusion. My conclusion was that it was the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you are saying that out of 30 men, only two wore the same uniform.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: That's how they were dressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And then they took you to the SUP building in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Some of them did. A group, not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then when you came to the SUP building, as you say in paragraph 11, Captain Petrovic, an officer of the JNA, came out and asked Dragan why he had brought you to the SUP building. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And after he went back to the building and came out again about half an hour later, he asked you with a smile whether you wanted a juice or a coffee; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he said you were going to the Posavina Hotel.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: That's where they took us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Posavina Hotel. Who took you there; the same men who brought you to the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: No; people who were some sort of security detail around the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they, too, wear different uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: No. They were uniformly dressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But they were not JNA soldiers either?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: I don't know what they were. I know how they were dressed, I know how they introduced themselves and who their leader was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did they introduce themselves and who was their leaders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Captain Dragan, and they were his volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In any case, they were not JNA. According to my information, Captain Dragan was never in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, but beyond any doubt those were not JNA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Well, those men were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you came to the Posavina Hotel you also noticed some armed men wearing dark blue overalls; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And now you claim that these dark blue overalls were actually the uniforms of those Dragan's volunteers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Well, that's how they spoke of themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They wore these dark blue overalls as uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Are we talking about soldiers or volunteers?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Call them as you like. You say that they wore dark blue overalls, and a moment ago you said they wore all kinds of clothing and no more than two were dressed the same.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Well, I expected that question. I knew you were going to ask that. Captain Dragan went from house to house arresting people accompanied not by his own men but by other men from other groups and other units. He was not accompanied in my part of town by his own men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You explained it now as you saw fit. But if his volunteers or members of his unit all wore those dark blue uniforms, how do you explain the fact that only their commander did not wear that uniform but wore jeans and military shirt instead? His entire unit wears the same uniform and he wears some sort of casual mixture.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: I don't want to go into their dress code, but I don't know what exactly their objective was; to occupy the town as fast as possible, to loot as much as possible. In any case, his men secured the SUP building and he was accompanied on his rounds by other men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You've told us quite enough for us to make our own conclusions. In paragraph 16, you say that when you were going to the toilet in the hotel, through a window --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Sorry, not a window, a door.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, a door. You noticed four dead bodies piled up on top of each other.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since they were piled up, I suppose they were brought there from somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How was it then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Let me be clear: Myself and the group I was in were the third group brought to the hotel that day. Those people must have been from the previous groups, because they were recently killed. The bodies were still bleeding, it was fresh blood. And the rest of the people were being driven towards the garrison and in other directions. Some were taken towards Loncari, which is towards the turn-off for Banja Luka, or to Brdjani, and one group was even taken towards the Rasnjevo village, which is about 30 kilometres away in the direction of Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. 1011. Please bear in mind that I'm asking questions only on the basis of your written statement because you have not testified before. And I'm asking you about these four men. How did you decide that they had been killed in that spot? Is it on the basis of the vapour emanating from the bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: I can say with a clear conscience that they were killed there. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Groups were either taken out of that hotel as a group or perhaps if somebody offered resistance or had a quarrel with those troops, they would be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, it was the 4th of May. It must have been rather warm. Could that have been the cause of that steam, that vapour you noticed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: What are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The 4th of May, it must have been warm. There could have been no outward sign, no vapour.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: The temperature of the body is higher than the outside temperature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is something we can easily establish. So that's what you saw when you saw those four bodies. Why didn't you write it in your statement? Although you said yourself that you didn't write your statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Well, I can't write English if I don't speak it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The statement I'm looking at is in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: It's a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you speak English?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You spoke Serbian?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And they were writing in English?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: I suppose they have an interpreter who does the interpreting for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say: "While we were detained in the hotel, we were allowed to use the toilet of the hotel. Once when I went to the toilet, I was able to look outside through a door that leads to the yard. I saw four dead bodies piled on top of each other. They were all men wearing civilian clothing."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say: "I was unable to identify a single one of them."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Could they have been brought from somewhere else after all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you allow for the possibility that those could have been bodies of some Serbian fighters who had been killed in combat because that hotel was under Serb control and they could have brought some of their men who were killed in combat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: No, by no means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Because you didn't recognise anyone. You say so yourself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: I could not identify them because they were piled on top of each other, on each other's stomach.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm only saying that you did not identify anyone, and still you don't allow for the possibility that they had been brought there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: They were certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear any shots prior to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: In town, where I came from, there was only shooting for the purpose of marking individual positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear shooting in town, in the hotel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If you didn't hear shooting in the hotel and you found those dead bodies there, they could not have been killed at the hotel without being shot, and you didn't hear any shots while there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: I'm telling you again, I was in the third group that was brought there. Two groups were brought there before us. So it is sufficient to know this to reject any possibility of those bodies being brought there from somewhere else. They were killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that when you came to the hotel you didn't go straight to the toilets. You must have been there awhile before going to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Thirty or 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So let's say it was 40 minutes. And in those 40 minutes, you didn't hear any shots. And then when you were passing by a door, you saw those four bodies. They could not have been killed in the hotel in the 40 minutes prior because you didn't hear any shots.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: They were not killed in those 40 minutes, but they were killed before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And they were still bleeding. That means that somebody brought them there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: That's not true. That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. 1011. Let's get one thing clear: You didn't hear shots while you were at the hotel, and you were there for at least 40 minutes before seeing those bodies.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes. Around 40 minutes, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Fine. And then you say in paragraph 17 that: "Goran Jelisic came at that point into the hotel accompanied by another resident of Brcko, a woman named Monika."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They were both local Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Monika was a local. She was born and lived there. Goran Jelisic was not from Brcko. He had come from Bijeljina some days prior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was tried here. We know where he came from. So it is not in dispute. His origin is not in dispute. So both of them were from that area; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Well, they were from Bosnia. Towns 50 kilometres away, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So although they were armed like the three soldiers who came with them, they wore different uniforms too. They were wearing parts of different uniforms; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: That was characteristic anyway for most of these people who were in Brcko on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That means that Jelisic or this Monika or the other persons who were present or the persons who came with them were not members of the JNA. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Probably not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And you claim that Jelisic was very upset because some of his friends had been killed in the fighting that took place in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: I cannot claim that, that they were killed, but they were stopped. They were not allowed to reach the Brcko hospital, and the road from the hospital towards Banja Luka would have been free then. That is Belgrade-Bijeljina-Banja Luka, the road that goes only through Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now you say that you cannot say whether they were or not, but here you said Jelisic was very angry. And later on, those who were with him said to you that some of their fellow combatants were killed when they were trying to push the Serb line across the bridge near the hospital. So the question I put to you was based on what you wrote here, that several of his comrades got killed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: I am stating what they did. I mean -- or what they said, these soldiers that came with Goran Jelisic. Then this fighting broke out, these men were beaten up, the men who were standing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you allow for the following possibility, that the persons killed you referred to a short while ago were the persons who got killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they were not the ones who got killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you preclude that possibility completely?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How come?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Because he became so angry, and we had seen these people before he had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, so you did not see them before.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Before he came to see us and before he started beating people, we saw these men. In my opinion, they were waiting for him to come to see what they do with us. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you preclude the possibility of these people being precisely the people who got killed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: I think that this is just a trick they tried to play because they did not manage to take this road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you say in paragraph 25, when they took you to the terrace of the hotel, you noticed that Jelisic had a pistol on him in a holster.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Wait a minute. He had a pistol, whereas Monika had that so-called Skorpion. Let's get this clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So Jelisic was armed by a pistol, and Monika had a Skorpion.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you saw Jelisic beating two Muslims with a truncheon.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes, he did have a truncheon in his hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And soon after that, you witnessed the killing of Sadik Ljaljic, a Muslim from Brcko.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who killed Sadik Ljaljic? Did you see these people who did that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: The people we just talked about, the people who were guarding the SUP building in the dark blue overalls, those men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when did that happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: That happened on the 4th of May. It could have been around 1.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where were you then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: On the terrace of the old hotel, in front. This terrace can be seen until the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where was this Ljaljic who had been killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: He was taken out of his house. His house is the second house behind the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute. You say that these were people in dark blue overalls and that they were the ones who did it. Why do you say in paragraph 28 that this was done by people who were commanded by Dragan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: I can say why: Because they themselves said that they were Captain Dragan's volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Those who killed this man called Ljaljic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since they took you away from the terrace and sent you to the park nearby --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- you say that a certain Mile Gatarevic walked up to you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Otherwise, a resident of Brcko, a man from your town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: With two other men.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, this Gatarevic didn't wear a uniform either; he was wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he was not a member of the JNA either.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes, he was not. I assume that he wasn't even a reservist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since he asked you to come with him, you did that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And at the moment when you were entering the SUP building --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- which is about 50 metres away from the hotel --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- you heard a burst of gunfire from the hotel terrace?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You instinctively looked then in the direction of the place where the gunfire was heard and you noticed Jelisic standing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: What are you saying? I did not say "whole," I said "group."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh. So you claim that he actually killed them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, did you say a short while ago that he was armed with a pistol only?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes, but he took from Monika this other pistol, this Skorpion, while we were still there, while we were standing on the hotel terrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So he took somebody else's weapon and killed these people.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: The two of them closely cooperated, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then allegedly you saw these people fall to the ground.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me try to get this straight. As you were entering the SUP building, you heard a burst of gunfire.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this man said to you that you shouldn't turn around, the man who was leading you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Well, he warned us not to turn around so that we would not be too noticeable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But when you did turn around by way of a reflex you noticed Jelisic with a weapon in his hand standing by the group of people who were also standing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't see him shooting.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: That moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I mean when you turned around. Did you see him as he was actually shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Wait a moment. I have to explain this. The moment I heard a burst of gunfire, I turned around and I saw Goran with this automatic pistol, and I saw people falling. No one else was shooting, no one around him. Everybody received orders from him while I was still there that if anybody tried to do anything, to move an arm, leg, whatever, that they should be killed on the spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have two minutes left, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, all right, I'll try to deal with everything within those two minutes, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that people who were standing in two lines were on the terrace of the hotel.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: The group that I stood in consisted of two lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that this group that was allegedly killed by Goran Jelisic were people who stood in two lines.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you see him take this weapon from this Monika?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: While I was still standing in line, before I was separated in the park.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 35, you say that at that moment Jelisic was on the terrace next to the dead men, the executed men.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you heard the burst of gunfire.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: He stood in front of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In front of them? But you did not see him shoot them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Well, I said this very nicely: The moment I heard the burst of gunfire, I turned around by way of a reflex, and I saw Goran standing there with an automatic pistol, and I saw people falling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But in the next sentence you say that the other soldiers were standing on the ground. This is only two steps below the place where Jelisic was. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And there is a footpath by the terrace. The terrace is on ground level, so it is only two steps above the ground, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So was he on his own or was he not on his own? According to what I heard from you and what I read here, he was not alone, there were at least ten armed men along with him. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Please, I said this a short while ago and I'll say it again: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Goran Jelisic stood on the Terrace with Monika. Below him, two steps below, on the footpath, which is not even five metres away from the park, there were people standing there who were also armed and who received orders from him that if anybody tried to do anything, they should be killed. So he was doing what he had intended to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Soon after the talks at the SUP building you were released, you were allowed to go home.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody beat you at the SUP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you spend a month at home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: I spent about two and a half months at home after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. This must be your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So after that, you were allowed to go home, immediately after that interrogation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were not beaten there and you stayed at home for another two and a half months?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you claim that you were then sent to the camp of Batkovic where you spent three months and then you were released from there too.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. Let me be quite clear. They came to me to sort of make a survey of apartments because I was staying at my parents' house -- at my sister's place, actually, which was nearby. That's where they found me. I was not in my own apartment. Also when they came on the 4th of May and when they collected us, they said that they were collecting us in order to take us to work somewhere near Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic -- Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Witness, just a couple of brief matters. I'm looking at paragraph 17 of your statement in English, and you describe Goran Jelisic at the hotel with Monika, and they had firearms and were wearing military clothing, and I'll read it out to you. If you'll just concentrate to the question, Witness, it will help you. "Jelisic was angry," and you were told later by the men that he'd lost some comrades during an attempt to push the Serb line across one of the bridges in the direction of the hospital. Can you assist the Court by telling us what exactly was happening there as it seems that there was some kind of conflict or confrontation. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: At that time when Goran returned, both he and his fellow combatants - let me not use another word - informed us that they'd tried to go in that direction, to take that road, and that they were actually stopped by some group of people, and they say that they even sustained casualties. I mean, if they had any dead, they would have brought them there for everyone to see, because this was a major slogan of theirs, that they were being killed, and they weren't doing anything else really. They didn't succeed in doing this, and they took out all their anger on the people who had been brought there. Quite simply, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And just turning now to paragraph 19, and it's on the same issue as to killings and confrontation. At the end of that paragraph, you say they were referring to an incident where Serbian soldiers were killed. Are you able to give any assistance to the Court as to what that was about, what was being referred to where Serbian soldiers were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: In terms of everything I've been saying so far and in terms of my testimony, I've been saying that they were trying to take the road between Belgrade-Bijeljina-Banja Luka. I repeat this is the only road going through Brcko. There's not any other road, and there's no shorter road either. So that is why they were taking this road. Or, rather, they were trying to take this road in order to link Krajina with Eastern Bosnia and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And are you able to assist as to who the fighting was between then when these people were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: That is what they were saying, that some people got killed, but specifically Goran Jelisic with his group of men tried this breakthrough, but then there were these other people, too, who know very well every street, every house, every shrub in town. So they stopped them, and they didn't allow them to take the road. That is why they came back angry. What they did, they did; they killed these people on the terrace of the old hotel, the old hotel called Posavina, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Witness, you have mentioned that the JNA came because they wanted to prevent conflict. When they came, how much fighting was going on in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Since I lived there before and then I'm not aware of any fighting. There were various attempts by way of provocations, but all of this was done on the part of people who had come to the military garrison of Brcko where they were put up. These were people who had special training, who were armed. They even slept there, and they went on orders to different parts of town in order to patrol these areas or to check things out. I cannot claim that there weren't any squabbles or skirmishes between them, including gunfire; but killing, no. When these special units came to town, that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you mentioned that these Serbian paramilitaries were staying with the JNA command in their barracks. Were they still staying there after the shooting incident you saw Jelisic commit outside the hotel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Yes. They had dormitories made available to them, military dormitories. That's where they slept, that's where they gathered. And from there they were sent on to various assignments, offensives, battles.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that Jelisic came from Bijeljina. Can you name any other paramilitary leader who came from Bijeljina who you also saw in Brcko at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: There was this person called -- I mean, he had this nickname Mauzer. I don't know his name. I don't even know his last name. But everybody, everybody, even his own men, called him by his nickname Mauzer.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And do you know -- well, you've mentioned that you knew the person who blew up the bridges. Do you know which political party he was a member of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Well, all of them opted either for the Serb Radical Party or the Serb SDS, as it was called, the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And was anyone injured when the bridge was blown up, that you know of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: Oh, and how. There were people who were crossing the bridge. This was just before the May holidays, so people were coming on buses from the Croatian side to the village of Gunj. They crossed this bridge which had been made as some kind of hanging bridge, and then buses awaited them on our Bosnian side and took them to different parts of Bosnia. These people got killed. Their number can only be estimated. But the fact is that they all ended up at this very unpopular place, that is to say the dog pound.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And do you know what the ethnicity was of these people who were injured? Were they largely from one ethnic group or both?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1011
utterances.text: I didn't know, because it is a well-known fact that in the former Yugoslavia, May Day was a holiday celebrated by everyone, irrespective of ethnicity or religion. Everybody celebrated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: That completes my re-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness B-1011, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go. Would you just wait until the blinds are pulled down before you do. We will now adjourn for half an hour. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Pack, just before we go into the witness, we need to consider the timing. There is legal argument. It had been arranged more conveniently than I arranged it to deal with that now, but I have arranged otherwise. But let us deal with it now. Mr. Kay, how long do you anticipate you might be?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'll be ten or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And Mr. Nice, depending of course on the argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course. I hope not very long -- I hope not very long because it's covered in pleadings. There are also associated pleadings which would probably best be read into the record to guide you, in both Krajisnik and in Brdjanin, so I would have thought no longer than Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So if we allowed three-quarters of an hour, that should be --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. Music, would you give the court, please, your name.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: My name is Mehmed Music. I was born in Donji Hadzici, near Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Could the witness be handed the bis package, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, have you made one statement to officers from the Tribunal in June of 1997?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And did you make two statements to authorities in Bosnia in April 1993 and in February 1998?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity since being in The Hague to read those three statements through in your own language?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: And are the contents of those statements true to the best of your knowledge, subject to a change which I shall deal with in a moment?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, one of those statements was the subject of a declaration pursuant to 92 bis. They were all part of an application under that rule, so I would ask instead that they are all admitted under Rule 89(F) of the Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution Exhibit number is 615.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'll read a short summary of those statements. Mehmed Music, a Muslim, lived in the village of Musici in the Hadzici municipality of Sarajevo at the outbreak of hostilities in Bosnia. He was captured after his village was attacked and shelled by Bosnian Serb forces. In his statement, he talks about the detention of large numbers of Muslim civilians, including women and children, in a series of detention facilities around Sarajevo from the 20th of May, 1992. He describes killings, interrogations, beatings and other mistreatment, including the imposition of forced labour of detainees in these facilities. He describes the presence of men he describes as Arkanovci at the sports hall in Hadzici and their beating and other mistreatment of detainees there. On the 22nd of June, 1992, Mr. Music was taken, along with approximately 280 detainees, to Lukavica barracks. He and 47 other men from his village area were forced to run a gauntlet of armed Serbs wearing red berets. He could tell from their manner of speech that the men wearing red berets were not from Bosnia. The witness, along with the other prisoners, was beaten as he ran the gauntlet. He came to a room where he saw the other detainees who had run the gauntlet before him lined up against the walls. There were officers at a desk in the middle of the room. One of the officers was wearing a cap which contained insignia similar to those of Serbia. Another one of the officers spoke with a Montenegrin accent. The officers sent the witness back through the gauntlet, telling him they hadn't called his name. The 47 other men, who included the witness's brother, have never been seen or heard of again. The witness describes seeing regular JNA soldiers at the Lukavica barracks during the time of his detention there and the presence of men he describes as Arkanovci. He also describes seeing armed men arriving from Serbia and Montenegro for the weekends, leaving on Mondays. These men, referred to as "weekend Chetniks," could be identified as being from Serbia and Montenegro by their speech. Your Honour, I have a few additional questions I'd ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown, please, his statement to the Tribunal at tab 1 of the bundle. In the bis package. If he could be pointed to his statement dated June 1997. It's the second statement in the bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, please look at paragraph 8 of the B/C/S version of your statement. You talk there about an incident in March 1992 occurring in the field near your property. Would you like to take this opportunity to correct the date that you speak to in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC
