utterances.text: Momo Stanimirovic is from Serbia. He is also from Serbia. And I know when Kasim Dermisevic and Sehic, he has two last names, he told us that it was this Stanimirovic who beat him up. We had to feed him through a straw. They just threw him on the ground. He lay there on the pallets. He was not able to move. He was beaten by those two men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know their full names, this Milos Cerovina, is he also from your area?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milos Cerovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was from Cerovik. And when they took us to the toilets to beat us up --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm only asking if he's a local resident.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. His sister worked with me in the Coca Cola company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From that garage they took you to a sports hall.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in the first statement, paragraph 3, you say that the warden was a certain Momo Vujovic, and then you gave the names of Ignjatovic, Mihajlovic, Kuzman --

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- Djokic, Krajisnik. They were the guards. All of them without any exceptions are from your area; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Momo Vujovic worked with me for 15 years in Coca Cola.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking about any one of them individually. All these people I mentioned are from your area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This Djokic is not from our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where is he from?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. When you're talking about what happened at the sports hall in Hadzici, you say that among the persons present you recognised a certain Fific and a certain Ljilja, a music teacher; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't recognise him. He was recognised by a Bosniak called Salihic. I don't know his first name. He was in camp with us later. And he was in a privileged position. He's the only one who they didn't beat. He kept him and he said all the others should be killed, all this scum except for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this Fific and Ljilja, you call them Chetniks on this page.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were others who came with them who had cream on their faces, gloves, what have you, not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But in paragraph 46 you call them Arkan's people, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what Momo Vujovic said to us. We said, Why did you let them beat us? We know each other. There was Sohic Ibro, a colleague who was also there with me. He said, How do we dare stand up to them, or how do we dare stand up to Seselj's men? They're going to kill us all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However in your second statement you say that you did not know Fific from earlier on and that he told you that these were Arkan's men.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I know him?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So finally, who are these people; Arkan's men, Chetniks? What are they?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me, they were hoodlums. That's what they were. They did the most terrible things. You just read up about all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your first statement you did not mention Arkan's men. Did somebody suggest to you that these may have been Arkan's men?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you. The first time, on the 22nd of May when I come back, they beat up Adem Nuhanovic [phoen] and his son. Adem died and his son is a sick person now because of all -- everything that he suffered. This young boy was 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you, Mr. Music, who made the suggestion to you that these were Arkan's men?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The guards said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, the guards?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because of course they didn't say, "We are from so-and-so."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How long were you detained and where were you in Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Slavisa Vajner Cica barracks in Lukavica from 1.00 onwards. We spent the night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, why do you not mention in the first statement this military barracks Slavisa Vajner Cica?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean I didn't mention it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see it in your statement. Maybe I made a mistake, but nowhere in your first statement did I manage to find any military barracks called Slavisa Vajner Cica.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not the only person there. 280 people were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you that. I'm asking you why you did not mention the military barracks or the soldiers in your first statement. What was the date when you were detained there in the military barracks?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 22nd of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well were these members of the army of Republika Srpska or the JNA on the 22nd of June?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 22nd of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The members of the JNA. And the berets were there, those guys from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 75 of your second statement you say that on -- or, rather, you said that on the 22nd of June, JNA soldiers were in Lukavica in the military barracks near Sarajevo. And in paragraph 75 of your second statement, you describe the mistreatment that you were subjected to you, you and your brother Miralem.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on the 23rd of June in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You do not mention that at all in your first statement?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean I don't mention it in my first statement? I can't forget that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you show me where you mention it in your first statement?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where the first statement is. You find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since I cannot find it, I'm asking you. I have the first statement, but you do not refer to the mistreatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, maybe I can be of assistance. This is in this version dated the 18th of April, paragraph 5 of the English version; and the Serb version, Mr. Music, page 3, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's in the second statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, what did you say it was?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The place that you referred to where your brother was mentioned, the third page, the last paragraph, where these persons were separated when you were singled out too. That is where it should be found.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it's not there. I talk about Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's not waste any time. It can be seen from the text.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then, as you stated, they swore at you, they beat you. You say you were beaten by officers. One of them wore a cap from the Lika area because you recognised the coat of arms of Lika on it. Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was from Serbia because I did my military service in Serbia at Pantelej Bubanj, so I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Lika is, though?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, I know Serbo-Croat, and I know how people speak in Serbia. He was swearing, everything he could think of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute. You say that he was from Lika and that he wore a cap from Lika. Does he talk the way people from Serbia talk or the way people from Lika talk?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was from Serbia. I'm 100 per cent sure. One was a Montenegrin officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But he was not from Lika.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not tell me where he was from. I didn't dare look at him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does this coat of arms of Lika look like, the one you say you recognised?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, you're really going into details now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you say that you saw the coat of arms of Lika. What does it look like?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, he said it. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, this man who wore this cap from Lika and the coat of arms of Lika, which army did he belong to; can you tell me that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know he was commander of the Red Berets, nothing else, because he kicked me later on. He kicked me in the rear, and he cursed my balija mother. He used the kind of words that people use in Serbia. He spoke Ekavian. I mean, come on. They worked with me in Germany for five years, people from Serbia and all of that. I mean, I have no reason to lie. Why would I say that they killed someone if I did not see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now look at paragraph 79, 80, and 82. You mention JNA officers, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: JNA soldiers came in and they said, "Who beat you?" And they were the ones who were in front of the doors, and they were not supposed to let anyone in. And when we were all beaten up and covered with blood, they said, "Who beat you?" And then they were using expletives. I don't want to say that here. And then in Lukavica I spent three nights actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These soldiers you mentioned here, they did not beat you, right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soldiers did not beat us; it's the Red Berets who beat us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute. They were with the soldiers. The soldiers did not beat you and then these men who were with the soldiers did beat you. Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They beat up my brother. He was half dead. I carried him in my own arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me something else, please: Were these JNA soldiers and they did not beat you? That's what you said. Or were they soldiers of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: JNA soldiers. They were in the hallway there and they were supervising us. However, they allowed these people who wore berets to get in and beat us, as well as Arkan's men. And they were supposed to protect us, guard us, but this was some kind of a trick. You know what that's like, it was a kind of a game.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, so it was a game; one group was beating you and others were trying to rescue you.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, like you and Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Music, in paragraph 117, you say that you were a member of the Commission for the Exchange of War Prisoners for the municipality of Hadzici from November 20, 1992 until June 30, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I imagine that while you worked for this commission you gathered a great deal of information about missing persons; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to talk about this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But do you have this information?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not for me to give it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, five minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No need, Mr. May. I don't even need those five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you, Mr. Music, how can we trust the information of that commission when you said so many contradictory things while you were making these statements here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a pure matter -- that's a pure matter of comment. The witness doesn't have to answer. Is there anything else you want to ask?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, nothing. Thank you, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Music?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you give another explanation in relation to your statement dated the 18th of April. If I understood you correctly a few minutes ago, you said that in this statement there was no mention of Arkan's men or of the Red Berets because that was mistranslated; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're talking about the 18th of April. Why are you talking about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of April, 1993, you gave your first statement. That is very close to the events that you describe.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And on the 18th of April, 1993, nowhere in this statement absolutely do you make any reference to Arkan's men or the Red Berets, and it is even more interesting to note that nowhere did you mention members of the Yugoslav People's Army. You only talked about Chetniks. Look at page 3, for example. I did the counting; you mentioned Chetniks 12 times, and you never mentioned the soldiers of the JNA or Arkan's men or the Red Berets. How can you explain that to the Judges that on the 18th of April, 1993, you absolutely did not mention them?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mention the 12th of April to you either of 1992 when 52 trucks came from Serbia, and in front of them were two tanks and two armoured vehicles and two combat vehicles. They drove through Hadzici and they went through the factory there, and then they went towards Crnovica [phoen] --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Music, that's not what I asked you.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just a minute, but I haven't told you about that either. And that's the main thing. And nobody dared stop them because they said, "We are doing whatever we want to do and whichever way we want to do it."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Music, but we haven't got much time. You gave this statement to the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is the statement that you gave to the security services of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You explained all these things to them, everything that you experienced, everything that you went through, and you never mentioned Arkan's men or the Red Berets or the members of the JNA anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It cannot be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Look at the statement you gave on the 16th in the month of June to the OTP. Now, what year was this? We don't know. Never mind. Look at paragraphs 16 and 17. You said here that on the 8th of May you saw -- some people, rather, said to you that they saw tanks and then there was serious shooting against you and also that tracers were used. Whose tanks were they, the ones that you mention in your statement to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of the JNA. If I had a tank, I wouldn't be sitting here now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Would you explain this to the Judges, please? How come you never mentioned those tanks in the statement that you gave in April, 1993 and all of a sudden, five years later, you refer to JNA tanks that you never mentioned before?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, I'm just going to tell you one thing: I don't even like to be reminded of all of this. There are people who have forgotten, even when they were detained or when they got out, and there were people who were asked in prison what their wives names were but they were so starved and so mistreated that they had lost their memory and couldn't even answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now please look at paragraph 75. You described in detail to the OTP everything that had to do with your brother. Miralem is your very own brother; right?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What you said here was: "As I was passing through this hallway, I saw a man who was lying on the ground. They told me to lift him. I saw that it was my brother Miralem. I brought him to a room and we ran the gauntlet in order to get to that room."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that what you said and is that the way it was?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please look at your statement of the 18th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that is paragraph 5 of that statement in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say in that paragraph you did not mention your very own brother anywhere. Nowhere whatsoever. And you did not talk officers, you talked about a Chetnik whose nickname was Crni Mrak, "pitch dark," and he beat you. How do you explain that? How come you never mentioned your very own brother in that statement? Because, after all, one's very own brother is something one cannot forget, especially if he lost his life there.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My very own brother was dead by then when Crni Mrak beat me. They lined us up. There was so much blood that you could step on. I had to keep my hands up here on my head, like this. And he was taller than me, he weighed a hundred kilos. He was taller than me by a head and I never heard of him again. They took them away. They probably took them to Pale and they burned them down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you don't have to explain this to me. Of course this is your brother, but then on the 18th of April when you were questioned by the security services, you did not talk about this most tragic thing that happened, that your brother lost his life then and there. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, I didn't say that he was dead there. Later on when we talked in camp, we heard about this, I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But that's not in your statement either.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot know where they took him. On the 23rd in the morning, they beat us up and they took 47 people and I was the 48th person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Just one more thing because I haven't got much time. I would like the Honourable Judges to assess this: You talk about Ljilja too who used to teach your daughters at the technical school. She used to teach a particular subject.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Music.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. When you mention Ljilja here - that is paragraph 3 of the English version, and you will find it in the first paragraph on page 3 - when you talked about Ljilja there, the music teacher who worked in Hadzici, you say Ljilja figured prominently because when any of the detainees would collapse on the floor from the beatings, she would jump on them. Do you remember having stated that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened right in front of my feet. She was jumping up and down on a man who was 70 years old, and the man cried. It was a terrible thing. Were they drugged? Were they drunk? I don't know what was wrong with them. They brought rifles, knives. What they did to people. I mean, they molested everybody. They made a man walk around the hall and to curse our Turkish mothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand, but look, when you made a statement five years later, you didn't say that any more. You said: "I recognised her because she used to teach my daughters at the technical school in Ilidza. I saw her taking off a man's trousers and telling another man to --" well, do something, something that has to do with sexual intercourse. I don't want to read this now in the interest of public morality. They had to do that.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So why did you not state it the first time and why was this heard much later, and other witnesses refer to it here? How come you didn't mention it then?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, how can you say that when this neighbour of mine is still alive? And what would it look like if I were to speak about that? Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How did she force him to do this? How did --

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She wanted to slit his throat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you did not talk about this earlier. Then she took off this man's trousers, and of course I'm not going to read this out because the Judges can read it.

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You did not talk about this earlier, so why are you talking about it now? Could you please explain that?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What have I got to explain to you? I mentioned everything in my statement and it's for the Judges to decide. It's not for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Very quick question in re-examination

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Mr. Music, it's been -- it may be that it's been suggested to you in your questioning by Mr. Tapuskovic and the accused that you have in your June 1997 statement made up what you said about Arkan's men, about the Red Berets, and the JNA tanks, and even the death of your own brother. Is that the case, that you made up this evidence in your June 1997 statement?

utterances.speaker: MEHMED MUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Your Honours, I did not make up anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... matter. That was the question. Yes. You were asked if you made anything up in your evidence to us, Mr. Music. Can you deal with that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Music, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Agha, time is rather short, but we'll see what we can do in terms of getting through as much as we can of this witness's evidence. Obviously the quicker you are, the better.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll try to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: So the Prosecution would call Witness B-1770, please. Your Honours, I believe he is a protected witness, so if I may ask for the blinds, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Agha, we can go to 3.40 with this witness. We can't sit beyond that, which may present difficulties in terms of timing.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: I can certainly be through my part very shortly, and if need be, the witness may have to come back, but hopefully we can see what we can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness would take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Witness B-1770, did you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecution on the 13th of March, 2002, which is now before you and signed by you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And is that your name on the front of the statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: May I please request the Chamber that this statement be admitted under 89(F) and be assigned an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 616, Your Honour, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. There is a proofing summary for this witness, but I intend just to very briefly skip over that so we can move along. In essence, this witness was a Bosniak who went to Srebrenica in 1993, where he experienced shelling from the Serbian side of the Drina. He then moved along to the Zepa enclave, and after the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves were taken in July 1995 by the Bosnian Serb forces, he swam over the River Drina and entered into Serbia. On reaching Serbia he was arrested by soldiers of the VJ, Yugoslav Army. He was then taken to two detention facilities but spent a period of about six months in the latter one. Whilst he was in such facility in Serbia, he was given insufficient food, water, he was beaten and was generally maltreated. Now, that, very briefly, is the essence of the witness's evidence, and that is the end of examination-in-chief, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If we could get through the witness, Mr. Milosevic, so much the better. If we can. If we can't, of course, then we will have to adjourn, but let's see how we get on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to make my cross-examination very efficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. B-1770, in the first paragraph of your statement you say that you decided to testify here because you were very angry when you heard that I stated here that we had saved 8 to 900 Muslims. I suppose you mean that brigade that swam across the Drina River and were admitted by our authorities who took care of them. Is that why you came here? Is that what made you angry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: I was not angry, I was indignant because I know how we were admitted and treated in that camp in Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The fact that you -- our authorities did admit that brigade of yours, which I think counted 840 people, if I remember correctly, is something different. You gave your statement on the 11th, 12th, and 13th of March, 2002 and less than a month before that proceedings started here concerning Kosovo not Bosnia-Herzegovina. How come that you heard this piece of evidence or my statement at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: I read somewhere this statement where you said that you saved 8 to 900 people from the Zepa enclave and you talked about some sort of admission centre, and I know exactly how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is easy to establish, because the entire international press corps visited the men from that brigade and all that was stated was stated in the presence of international media representatives. I'm asking you how is it possible that you were indignant on the 11th of March when the proceedings here were only about Kosovo? There was no mention of Zepa, Bosnia, or anything of the kind.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: I heard your statement on television in which you said that you had rescued 8 to 900 men, including me, but I know exactly what kind of rescue that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I'm asking you. How were you able to know that before the 11th of March when the proceedings here concerned only Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: There was talk about Srebrenica as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Never mind. That's easy to establish. Can you remember, perhaps, when I made that statement? How long was it between that statement and your indignation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: then. And they told me you can only go there and say so on the spot. They gave me the telephone number of Tribunal, and I called and applied to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That could not have been your motive because there was no talk about Bosnia then. That was, however, the first reason you gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let's not waste too much time arguing about this kind of point. He's given his reason and given his explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I hope it is not in dispute that this explanation cannot be truthful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the second motivation you allege here for your decision to testify and that is that you had no freedom of movement because you are not allowed to go back to the place where you used to live.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 1770, where are you residing now? Where did you live when you gave that statement to the investigators in March 2002?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: (redacted) tell me, who is it who restricted your freedom of movement and did not allow you to go back to where you used to live?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Your co-combatants, the people who live there, the people who expelled me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So after the war, you were not able to go back to your hometown?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: I did not. I did not dare to. And even now I don't dare to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Because I have been through all kinds of things during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The consequences are still there, and some people have come to positions they should not have occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to understand your motivation. Your real motivation does not seem to be to coincide with the reason you state here. Is it true that you came back to Bosnia in August 1996? (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is my impression correct that you were in fact forced to do that job? You did not do it of your own free will? You were designated, assigned to that job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: I was not assigned. I was hard up for money, I had no job, and I had to earn money somehow to keep my family alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you perhaps designated to do this job because you were treated by the BH army as a deserter precisely because in July 1995 you deserted and found refuge in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: I did not desert. We were expelled. All of us from the enclave of Zepa and the enclave of Srebrenica were driven out. We were not deserters and were not treated as such.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Yes, it was in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that you got an eviction order to leave the house which you occupied.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Yes. I received this eviction order. I had to live in this abandoned house. I had no other way, except to Republika Srpska where I did not dare go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that was in the area controlled by the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so it was the Muslims who expelled you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: No, it was not the Muslims, it was the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. The rules. Then in the year 2000 you asked for asylum and you left Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you and your family did not leave Bosnia and Herzegovina because of Serbs but because of the attitude of your own authorities towards you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Sir, in view of the fact that I am from a town called Bijela, which is now within the Serb entity of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina and I was expelled as a non-Serb after all the things I had gone through there under that government and during the war, I shudder at the mere thought of going back. My own child was killed, I don't even know where he is buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm very sorry to hear that, sir. But you were not really expelled from that house in the territory of Republika Srpska, which is what you call a Serb entity. It was in the territory of the Federation, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: There is another reason. Another reason is that I cannot return to my own property, to the place where I used to live and work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But in Bosnia and Herzegovina you are allowed to reside.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in paragraph 73, you say that you cannot go back to Luka, which is the municipality of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: It was in the municipality of Srebrenica, but it belonged to the Zepa enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the reason is fear.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Great fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me. Why didn't you go back to some other town in the territory of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina outside of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Sir, the Dayton Accords set such rules to prevent ethnic cleansing. I was a former camp inmate with all the bad experience of living there that I had. I had lived for four years under siege, and even now there are the same troops that had driven us out, and the people who treated us like cattle. I shudder at the mere thought of going back. It's impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You claim that you are an expelled person, that you spent time in some sort of camps in Serbia, that you are a person who got injured on a very high-responsibility job that you were doing for the benefit of your own state, and you say you are not allowed to go back to your own country. Why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: I gave you my reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In some of the first paragraphs of your statement where you describe the general situation in the area of Srebrenica, Bratunac, and Luka, where you lived until July 1995, you describe in various ways your fears and misgivings in relation to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: That's true. Radovan Karadzic is still at large.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. Tell me this: You who were so afraid of Serbs in Bosnia, you say the terrible things happened there, and of course war is a terrible thing. How come that you decided to go to Serbia and seek cover and refuge there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Sir, I made that decision together with a man who worked for an enterprise in Serbia. We made our plans together, and we planned to pass unnoticed via Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you were not together with that brigade that swam across the Drina River and who were admitted by our authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: It was not a brigade. It was men, women, and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were not a part of that brigade that was admitted by our authorities after swimming across the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: If I had, I would be in the Sljivovica camp in Mitrovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Never mind. We'll establish that easily. In paragraphs 23 and 24, you described the reasons why you decided to leave the Zepa enclave and to go straight to Serbia, where, as you say, you were threatened the most. Tell me, how large were the forces of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina that were present in Zepa when you decided to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, why did you decide to run away from Serbs to Serbia, leaving behind your family, wife and three children, if there were no Serbs in Zepa at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: They arrived. They torched the surrounding villages, came in, transported women and children, and we were left at their mercy. Since it was a UN protected area and the people were disarmed, even the people who used to have weapons, I came across people who had survived the tragedy of Srebrenica, who were going back from the free territory in Tuzla. They told me about the terrible things they had survived, and I had no thought of going to the free territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, were you running away from the Serbs or were you running away from the possibility of being mobilised into the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: I was running away from -- from criminals and villains but Serb villains.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There were many directions in which you could have run away, but you chose one which was controlled by Serbs, unlike many others. Was it possible to go elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: No, not at the time. It wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 24, you say that, "I decided to go my own way so as to give at least one of us a chance of surviving."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: I was together with my three brothers, and I heard stories from the survivors of Srebrenica about all the dangers that were awaiting us, and I decided that we should split so that at least some of us should survive, because I was almost certain, 99 per cent certain, that we would all get killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You wanted to survive, at least some of you, but you had a wife and three children.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: I think that it was on the 25th. They were transported to the free territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this happened before you decided to escape to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this large group of combatants from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, 840 of them who found refuge in Serbia, were motivated by their desire to avoid fighting in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina any longer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Our objective was to stay alive; to find peace somewhere and to stay alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In many places in your statement, you refer to torture that you were exposed to in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I absolutely assert that it cannot be true. Tell me, when conflicts began in your region, you said that you weighed 85 to 90 kilos. That's in paragraph 5 of your statement. And in the same paragraph, you say that on the 2nd August, 1995, when you were allegedly arrested in Serbia, you weighed 96 kilos.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Close to that. Close to my arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that's in paragraph 35, not 5. You say that you lost 30 to 35 kilos during your detention in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. 1770, you were given a permit to travel issued by the High Commissioner of -- High Representative for Refugees in Srebrenica, and your photograph is under tab 2. I won't put it on the ELMO because you're a protected witness, but I would like to draw the attention of all those who can look up tab 2. You gentlemen obviously don't have it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that you in the photo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: I had my passport in my pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What it says here, United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, Provisional Travel Certificate. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Your name is stated here, and then it says, "Office of the Chief of the Mission in Yugoslavia," all your details are indicated and your photograph is here.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you have that document in your pocket?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please be so kind to look at it, then. That photograph was taken in early December 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Correct. In fact, I don't know exactly when it was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I suppose it was taken when this paper was issued, around the 8th of December, 1995.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Yes. Based on this photo, and the details of your height - all this is written in the travel permit - one can calculate very precisely your weight at the time when this photograph was taken. I don't see the face of an emaciated man who had been starved. I see a relatively well-nourished person. Do you have anything to say to this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: When the people from the Red Cross weighed us, I told them that I had lost a lot of weight. I weighed 50 something kilos. And one of the people who were there told me, "Don't worry, we'll fatten you up." And that's what really happened. Humanitarian aid arrived. They increased our rations, they gave us some ten biscuits of some military-type rations per day, and when it was all over, I was surprised to see how much weight I really gained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the case as you describe it is that you were first starved, lost a lot of weight, and then gained back some weight before you got this travel permit. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that your now late President Izetbegovic said, when all of you, the entire brigade, fled to Serbia - and obviously you were not there because you said you went with some other man to Skopje - he said that we should hand you all over to the authorities.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: I did not know that the then-President Alija Izetbegovic asked for us to be returned, because we did not have any communications, any information, no newspapers, radio, nothing. We didn't even dare look around the facilities where we were staying let alone listen to something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not going to be a problem, these 840 persons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: No. There was about 950 of them, because there were about 800 in Sljivovica, and others were at the other camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean you were staying at Mount Tara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: We passed that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about this unit that swam across the Drina River? The entire diplomatic corps went to see it on the very next day, after they swam over the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: What do you mean diplomatic corps? What is this corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Diplomats accredited in Belgrade from dozens of embassies.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: That's right, we were visited by them, yes. They came with truncheons. Oh, didn't we have a good time when they came.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So Izetbegovic and his government were informed about the fact that you swam across. And I publicly stated that you were free to leave Serbia and go wherever you wished to go, to any country.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know what you stated. I don't know whether anybody was looking for us, I mean the government in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I just know what happened to us there, that we were not informed about anything or, rather, that we were not entitled to receive any information. I didn't have the right to see my nephew who was underage and he was at the next-door facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that all of these men, and I don't have a list here, this list was made at that time by the international organisations, but all of those who were in the territory of Serbia then who had crossed to the territory of Serbia on that occasion were always under the supervision of the International Red Cross? And there is not a single official complaint in respect of your treatment or the treatment of other Muslims who were part of this large group. As far as I can remember, it was 840 men that swam across the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: I find this ridiculous. It was terrible. A young boy underage, 15. I think he died in this camp where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You yourself say in paragraph 41 that the Serb authorities brought representatives of the International Red Cross to your room.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To show them how they took good care of you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Yes, precise. It was an equipped room, a room equipped with beds in order to be shown to the Red Cross and the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they moved about freely in other rooms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Well, later, about three months later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. No. They were there from the very first day. That can even be seen from the newspaper. So what was it that was concealed from the members of the International Red Cross; bruises, malnourishment? This was never established by members of the International Red Cross. How could this have been concealed from them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: That's right. They were not given proper access to Sljivovica I think for about three months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if I may make this observation: You mentioned this incident that you saved the 840 people during the opening statement in February 18th of last year. So when you asked about the witness's motive, so the witness may have referred to this, your statements of last year. So you said that you couldn't have mentioned this because the trial was on the Kosovo phase.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. Kwon. What matters here is that what I'm saying is the truth, that is rescuing these 840 men and taking care of them in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So are you able to give me the name and surname or rank or affiliation with some unit or the MUP or the army of Yugoslavia, the MUP of Serbia or the army of Yugoslavia of any person who you claim mistreated you or who behaved towards you in some way which was not in line with human dignity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Sir, they never introduced themselves to us. When we went out for breakfast, we had to run the gauntlet, and they would beat us with rifles butts. At any rate, they would beat us that way in the morning and in the evening. And also during the night they called out our names or they'd come to the door, and quite simply if they'd see anyone who was physically a bit more capable, they'd take them out into the hall and beat them, two or three men. And then also when they were taken downstairs by your men -- I remember Vlado Karadza, for instance, and Slavenko. Slavenko was a military man. During the first month, he was there around us all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that this is someone who beat you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Yes, yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you mentioned a name and it can be corroborated easily. Everything that has to do with this Muslim brigade is rather transparent anyway. Tell me, after leaving Serbia, did you undergo any kind of medical examination or any kind of check-up to see whether there were any traces of these alleged beatings that you had sustained in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: The International Red Cross people talked to us, sort of. We weren't examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is this when they came to see you when you were staying in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: In camp in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You were under constant supervision of the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: No. They came to see us twice a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you saw them every time and they saw you every time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: They brought us messages. They used to take us out. Sometimes then used to take us out of the room into the hall. They would give us messages and also tobacco.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, they brought you cigarettes and letters.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Yes, letters that had all sorts of things crossed out, things that somebody did not like, somebody who censored the letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody from the International Red Cross establish some kind of malnourishment or mistreatment during your stay in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Believe me, I didn't ask them. I believe that if they worked properly, that they did note this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have a shred of evidence for all this that you have been saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: For what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For what you're saying, that you were mistreated.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: I have a lot of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Well, that a man suffocated when travelling towards the camp of Sljivovica on a truck because there wasn't enough air. There were too many of us under the tarpaulin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. 1770, that with regard to this event that you are talking about here, there is a great deal of video footage, and also the direct observations of members of the diplomatic corps in Belgrade and many reports of international humanitarian organisations, and there is not a bit of what you've been saying here in any of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Well, there is evidence of that. I think it was your television, Television Serbia, that made a programme. A man had to read a thank you letter addressed to you - that was pitiful - saying that you were so noble.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, so you were not met there, saved, rescued. You were not taken care of, fed, but you were beaten. That's what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Exactly. It was a camp. It was a real camp, a torture camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. It is very good that you say that because there are so many documents about this. Just tell me one more thing: Who is the author of this report on refugees who fled to Serbia after Zepa fell? This is a report about refugees who fled to Serbia after Zepa fell. That is the Sandzak Helsinki Committee.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: I don't know that paper, I don't know where it came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, you don't know. All right, I'm not going to ask you anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 9th of December, 2001, you gave a statement to a certain Bjorn Johnson in Sweden; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Yes, yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Or Johnsson. I'm not very familiar with Swedish last names.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: A very nice man, a fine gentleman Mr. Bjorn Johnsson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Look at what it says here: "During the interview at the immigration office in Gothenburg -" I'm not going to give your name which is here - "he did not speak about the above-mentioned events. He only said that he had been in camps and then in the United States." So that is what it written here in what you say is a report of this fine gentleman. You did not write about the events that you spoke of here. It was just established that you had been in a camp there and then in the United States of America.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Yes, correct, because I have an ID from a camp and also a Red Cross ID. So they didn't ask for any explanations. This was sufficient proof for them, the ID and the certificate from the UNHCR and the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Just one more thing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I shall remain within the time frame that you asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On this page that has a particular ERN number and that was given to Mr. Johnsson: "Since he did not manage to transfer his family to the United States, he returned to Bosnia and sustained a wound due to a shrapnel. The family fled to --" and that was now redacted -- "in September 2000." So it can be seen here that you were fleeing from something in the Federation. Can you explain what that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Well, you see, it's quite correct. It can be seen that I left the Federation for the following reason: I cannot think of going back to the Serb Republic where I had lived before the war. I don't dare go there. However, the rules that exist now in Bosnia-Herzegovina say that people who lived in the Serb Republic before the war, if they lost their status or if they were not registered in the Federation have to return to the Serb Republic. Since I do not dare go there, I have no choice, so I had to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You weren't fleeing from anything in particular from the Federation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. 1770.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will really try to finish within a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in paragraph 26 you gave an explanation, but if I understood you correctly, you said that you were expelled from Bosnia and that you left Bosnia against your own will.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: The Serb Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 26, take a look. You said here: Six of us men decided to cross the driver. They were Alija Beganovic, his nephew Jasmin, who was 16 years old at the time. There were three other guys but I can't remember their names. So the six of you decided to cross the Drina, to swim across the Drina, and that's what you did.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now please look at paragraph 67: The ICRC started talking to us in December and they asked me where I wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I said as far away as possible and as soon as opinion. The ICRC representative never said anything to me because I don't think they really checked those papers at all. The first group of detainees, about 200, went to Australia. The second, of which I was a part, there were 112 or 120 of us, left for the United States. The third or last group - I don't know for sure - went to France. So whoever wanted to go could go wherever they wanted to go. Nobody prevented them from doing is that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: They could go with the assistance of the UNHCR and the Red Cross. They could go to third countries. There were people who wanted to return to Bosnia-Herzegovina, however, that was not possible for them. That is what the bosses at the camp said: Don't you dare think about that, no one can go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you did go where you wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Now, why did I say as far away as possible and as soon as possible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: I wanted to leave this torture and this terrible life as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But from Serbia, you were allowed to go wherever you wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: Who allowed me to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I might, very briefly, ask the witness just one question in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly ask him one question. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, it's been mentioned by the accused and amici that actually people were taken into Serbia who had swam across the Drina and they were actually treated quite well and you were free to go and you were looked after. Now, if I could just kindly -- I mean, before I come to this, and actually there's nobody who can sort of confirm or back up what you're contending, so if I could just refer you to your actual statement and tab number 3 of your package, if you'd kindly be provided with that. It's tab 4, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: If Your Honours are able to find this.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And this is actually an extract from the Helsinki Committee for Human Rights, which was annexed to the witness's statement. Now, could you just please very briefly read the three points which are mentioned, 1, 2, 3 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He said he didn't know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Well, it's actually in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, but during the cross-examination he said he didn't know this, but you can re-examine on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Could you just kindly read out that extract of the report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure about this. Do you know about this, Mr. 1770 or not? Do you know about this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The lawyer put this in front of me and asked me whether I knew the people from this list. He said to me how I should mark the persons I knew, that I should mark the names of those who I knew, and that's what I did. I also marked those who were my family members, relatives. I know quite a few of these people. All of these people are alive. They can talk just like I'm talking now.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And what does the report say, record about them, where they were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1770
utterances.text: This report pertains to a list of men who were in Sljivovica and Mitrovo Polje, the two camps, in 1995. It says that they were not in Sljivovica for a long time, or, rather, that they were not reported to the Red Cross on time, and also with the Helsinki Committee. Somebody made this list. I really have no idea who made this list. The only thing I was asked to do was to underline the names of the persons I knew from this list, the persons I knew personally. And I know quite a few of them because we were together, quite a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all, Your Honours. The list speaks for itself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness B-1770, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go. If you would just wait while the blinds are drawn. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is there no chance of two minutes in private session? Is it too late?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. A very short two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So, Witness, if you wouldn't mind waiting and we'll just go into private session for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 15th day of December, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.49 p.m.,
